doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
title: King Oliver, Kid Rena and Buddy Petit in the second line
summary: Barker followed his uncles' parades to hear Oliver, Rena and Chris Kelly, and says Buddy Petit drew the biggest following with diminished chords and Indian Sau Wau.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Did you see people like . . . and hear King Oliver and them perform before they went up to Chicago?
Yeah, second line with my uncles.

That’s right. See King Oliver. In those days we’d have maybe six or seven guys following right within hearing distance, not to disrupt the second line, to listen to King Oliver blow, wait until he play his chorus, and he’d blow it at them. “Hey Joe, put that riff in there.” Him and Kid Rena, he had his followers, and Buddy Petit had more followers than anybody.
The whole seventh ward would be listening to Buddy. He played them dimished chords. They had never heard nothing like that. Playing Indian Sau Wau [or Indian Sagua]. You know Indian Sau Wau?
Let’s see. [White tries to sing it.] Let’s see. It had a minor thing in it. I know. I know it. I heard . . . Bunk Johnson I think recorded it.
That was one of Buddy’s things.
Bunk played it. I think Punch [Miller] and George Lewis or somebody recorded
Maybe it was Kid Howard. Yeah. I really liked that. I want to start playing that.

It was dimished chords, and Buddy Petit run changes all on top of changes. [Barker sings a melody of that ilk.] He’d do all that, and they would [? (inaudible)] whoever was there [? (inaudible)], because they say he had fidgeties of the fingers. I heard [? (inaudible)] tell somebody, “a fidgety of the fingers.” Say, “His fingers is . . .” “Man, practice.” They thought it was, everybody, Wooden Joe [Nicholas] was pressing on one valve at a time. Here come Buddy Petit, making triplets.
